title: Researchers Screen 6,400 Drugs for Anti-Aging Potential Using Network Science
excerpt: A Northeastern University-led team mapped thousands of aging-related genes onto the human protein network and identified existing drugs that could reverse hallmarks of aging.
body:
• Researchers mapped 2,358 longevity-associated genes onto a network of over 500,000 protein interactions to find drugs that could target aging processes.
  • Aging-related genes cluster in specific neighborhoods of the human interactome rather than being randomly distributed — a finding that makes drug targeting feasible.
  • The team screened 6,442 existing drugs and identified 370 candidates that could affect one or more hallmarks of aging, with 14 showing potential to promote longevity.
  • A new metric called pAGE measures whether a drug reverses or accelerates age-related gene expression changes, addressing a gap in previous repurposing efforts.

A team led by researchers at Northeastern University has built a computational framework that screens thousands of existing drugs for their potential to slow or reverse biological aging — and found that some common medications, including an over-the-counter nasal spray, may warrant further testing as longevity interventions. The study was published in Nature Aging in June.

The researchers, led by physicist Albert-László Barabási and postdoctoral researcher Bnaya Gross, integrated 2,358 longevity-associated genes onto the human interactome — a comprehensive map of more than 500,000 protein-to-protein interactions — and then measured how close each of 6,442 clinically approved or experimental compounds from the DrugBank database sat to the gene clusters governing specific aging processes.

Aging Genes Aren't Random — They Form Neighborhoods

The study's foundational discovery is structural. Genes linked to each of the 11 recognized hallmarks of aging — processes like mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic alterations and declining cell-to-cell communication — don't scatter randomly across the protein network. They cluster into connected subgraphs the researchers call "hallmark modules."

"If the genes were spread randomly, there is no way for a drug to specifically affect it because it's spread all over," Gross told Northeastern Global News. "Our discovery is that aging genes are located in very specific areas, a very specific neighborhood, allowing you to find drugs that affect this neighborhood."

That clustering is what makes drug targeting viable. A compound doesn't need to hit an aging module head-on. It can work through network proximity — reaching the relevant genes through a direct path in the protein interaction map.

Measuring Direction, Not Just Proximity

Previous drug-repurposing efforts could predict whether a compound interacted with disease-related gene clusters, but not whether it helped or hurt. Gross and Barabási's team introduced a metric called pAGE (Pro-Age) to fill that gap. The metric compares a drug's effect on gene expression against the expression changes known to occur during aging. If a gene becomes less active with age, the goal is a drug that reactivates it. If a gene ramps up with aging, the drug should dampen it.

"As someone whose hair turned gray years ago, I share the universal wish that there might one day be a pill that slows aspects of aging. The challenge is figuring out which drugs are worth testing."

— Albert-László Barabási, Distinguished University Professor of Physics, Northeastern University

By combining network proximity with pAGE scores, the team identified 370 drugs with potential effects on one or more aging hallmarks. Fourteen showed promise for promoting longevity; another 14 appeared to accelerate aging-related changes. The researchers validated their approach against 17 drugs already in human longevity trials and 11 compounds shown to extend lifespan in mice.

From Nasal Spray to Longevity Candidate

Among the unexpected findings: oxymetazoline, an over-the-counter decongestant sold as Afrin or Sinex, emerged as a candidate for improving cell-to-cell communication — a process that degrades with age. The drug has no known longevity effects, but the framework's predictions are now being tested in cell-line experiments with collaborators at Harvard's Brigham and Women's Hospital, according to Gross. Aspirin, already in human trials for longevity benefits, was also flagged as a candidate for positively affecting cell-cell communication and nutrient sensing.

A Roadmap, Not a Cure

Barabási was careful to temper expectations. "This study does not provide a cure for aging, nor does it prove that any specific drug will extend human life," he said. "It offers a roadmap toward actionable interventions that can be tested in cells, animals and eventually humans."

The complexity of aging means a comprehensive strategy would likely require multiple drugs addressing different hallmarks simultaneously. Developing a new drug for each of the 11 hallmarks from scratch could take over a decade. Repurposing existing compounds — with known safety profiles and side effects — could compress that timeline sharply.

What This Means for Indian Pharma

India's generic pharmaceutical industry, which supplies roughly 20% of the world's generic medicines, is built on producing existing drug formulations at scale. A computational framework that systematically identifies new therapeutic uses for already-approved compounds aligns directly with that expertise. If drugs like oxymetazoline or aspirin prove effective in longevity trials, Indian manufacturers would be well-positioned to produce and distribute them globally — turning drug repurposing science into accessible, affordable interventions.

What's Next

Harvard cell-line experiments to validate the computational predictions are underway. Gross said the methodology could eventually be personalized — tailoring anti-aging drug recommendations to an individual's genetic profile, a concept the researchers call "precise geroscience." That remains aspirational. "I think we are not there yet," Gross said, "but we are moving toward the era of preciseness."
